gloss: A unit of time equal to one sixtieth of a minute.
examples: Give me a *second* to find my keys.
The whole thing took about thirty *seconds*.
He beat his old record by two *seconds*.

gloss: A unit of time equal to sixty seconds.
examples: The bus leaves in five *minutes*.
Do you have a *minute* to talk?
Wait a *minute* — that isn't what she said.
contrast: The noun is MIN-it, but the adjective *minute* (крошечный) is my-NOOT, with the stress on the second syllable.

gloss: A unit of time equal to sixty minutes.
examples: The flight takes about three *hours*.
She studies for an *hour* every evening.
We waited in line for half an *hour*.
contrast: The h is silent, so the word takes *an*, not *a*: an hour.

gloss: A period of twenty-four hours, or the light part of it.
examples: I'll call you in a couple of *days*.
What a beautiful *day* it is.
She works six *days* a week.

gloss: A period of seven days.
examples: We're going to Chicago next *week*.
The class meets twice a *week*.
I've been sick for two *weeks*.
contrast: *Week* and *weak* (слабый) are perfect homophones in American English.

gloss: One of the twelve periods that a year is divided into.
examples: My lease is up at the end of the *month*.
The baby is only three *months* old.
It rained almost every day last *month*.

gloss: A period of twelve months.
examples: She moved to Texas two *years* ago.
This has been a good *year* for the company.
He saved all *year* for the trip.

gloss: A period of ten years.
examples: The house hasn't been painted in *decades*.
She spent a *decade* teaching high school.
Crime has dropped over the past *decade*.
contrast: Stress the first syllable — DEK-ayd, unlike Russian «декАда». It also means ten years, not ten days.

gloss: A period of one hundred years.
examples: The church is more than four *centuries* old.
Photography changed art in the last *century*.
This bridge has stood for over a *century*.

gloss: A period of two weeks.
examples: They stayed with us for a *fortnight*.
The results come back within a *fortnight*.
He wrote to her every *fortnight* that summer.
contrast: Mainly British. Americans understand *fortnight* but almost always say *two weeks*.

gloss: An extremely long period of time.
examples: These rocks formed *eons* ago.
It feels like an *eon* since we last talked.
The river took *eons* to carve the canyon.

gloss: A long stretch of history with a particular character.
examples: The telephone opened a new *era* in communication.
That song belongs to a different *era*.
Both *eras* produced great architecture.

gloss: A distinct period in history or in the development of something.
examples: The moon landing marked an *epoch* in space travel.
Geologists divide the past into *epochs*.
We're living through an *epoch* of rapid change.
contrast: The ch is said like k, and the word is stressed on the first syllable — EP-uhk, unlike Russian «эпОха».

gloss: How old someone or something is, or a long period of history.
examples: She learned to read at the *age* of four.
Children under the *age* of twelve get in free.
It took *ages* to get through security.

gloss: All the people born and living at about the same time.
examples: My grandmother's *generation* saved everything.
The farm has been in the family for four *generations*.
This *generation* grew up with smartphones.

gloss: The whole length of a person's life.
examples: He saw the country change in his *lifetime*.
That was the trip of a *lifetime*.
The pan is supposed to last a *lifetime*.

gloss: The length of time a person, animal, or thing lives or lasts.
examples: A housefly has a very short *lifespan*.
Average *lifespans* have risen steadily.
The roof has a *lifespan* of about thirty years.

gloss: The length of time something continues.
examples: Please stay seated for the *duration* of the flight.
The *duration* of the course is six weeks.
He said nothing for the whole *duration* of the meeting.

gloss: A period of time between two events.
examples: Take one pill at four-hour *intervals*.
There was a long *interval* between the two storms.
Buses run at ten-minute *intervals*.

gloss: The length of time that something lasts or covers.
examples: She wrote four novels in the *span* of a year.
His attention *span* is about ten minutes.
The study covers a *span* of two decades.

gloss: A very short period of time.
examples: Could you wait a *moment*?
For a *moment* I thought he was serious.
We had a few quiet *moments* before the guests arrived.

gloss: An extremely short moment of time.
examples: The lights went out in an *instant*.
For an *instant* nobody moved.
She knew his voice the *instant* he spoke.

gloss: A very short time, used mostly in casual speech.
examples: I'll be back in a *jiffy*.
The soup heats up in a *jiffy*.
He had the tire changed in a *jiffy*.

gloss: A fixed period, such as a school session or a time in office.
examples: The senator is serving her second *term*.
Grades come out at the end of the *term*.
He signed on for a five-year *term*.

gloss: One of the two main periods that an American school year is divided into.
examples: I'm taking chemistry next *semester*.
She studied abroad for a *semester*.
Both *semesters* end with final exams.

gloss: One of three periods that a pregnancy or a school year is divided into.
examples: She felt tired all through the first *trimester*.
The baby grows fast in the third *trimester*.
That school splits the year into three *trimesters*.

gloss: A period spent on one activity, or a formal meeting.
examples: We booked an hour-long therapy *session*.
The legislature is in *session* until June.
The band recorded three *sessions* last week.

gloss: One stage in a process of change or development.
examples: The project is entering its final *phase*.
It's just a *phase* — he'll grow out of it.
The moon goes through eight *phases*.
contrast: *Phase* and *faze* (смущать, выбивать из колеи) sound exactly alike.

gloss: One step in a longer process.
examples: The illness was caught at an early *stage*.
We'll do the remodel in three *stages*.
At this *stage* nothing has been decided.

gloss: A series of events that repeat in the same order.
examples: The washing machine is running a short *cycle*.
The news *cycle* moves fast these days.
These insects have a two-year life *cycle*.

gloss: The part of the day from sunrise until noon.
examples: I drink coffee every *morning*.
The appointment is Tuesday *morning*.
Cold *mornings* make it hard to get up.
contrast: *Morning* and *mourning* (траур) are perfect homophones in American English.

gloss: The part of the day between noon and evening.
examples: Let's meet Friday *afternoon*.
She naps most *afternoons*.
It rained all *afternoon*.

gloss: The part of the day between the end of the afternoon and bedtime.
examples: We usually eat at six in the *evening*.
He teaches two *evenings* a week.
It was a warm summer *evening*.
contrast: Two syllables, not three — EEV-ning. The middle e is not pronounced.

gloss: The dark part of every twenty-four hours.
examples: The baby cried all *night*.
We stayed two *nights* in Denver.
Drive carefully at *night*.
contrast: *Night* and *knight* (рыцарь) are perfect homophones; the k and the gh are both silent.

gloss: Twelve o'clock at night.
examples: The store closes at *midnight*.
We talked until well past *midnight*.
The new rules take effect at *midnight*.

gloss: Twelve o'clock in the middle of the day.
examples: Checkout is at *noon*.
By *noon* the temperature hit ninety.
The parade starts a little before *noon*.

gloss: The middle part of the day, around twelve o'clock.
examples: The heat is worst at *midday*.
We took a *midday* break in the shade.
By *midday* the fog had burned off.

gloss: The time when light first appears in the morning.
examples: The crew set out at *daybreak*.
Birds start singing before *daybreak*.
We hiked from *daybreak* until dark.

gloss: The time when the sun goes below the horizon.
examples: Be home before *sundown*.
The temperature drops fast after *sundown*.
They fish from dawn to *sundown*.

gloss: The hours between sunrise and sunset.
examples: Raccoons rarely come out in the *daytime*.
*Daytime* temperatures are staying near freezing.
He works nights and sleeps in the *daytime*.

gloss: The hours of darkness.
examples: *Nighttime* is when the bakery gets busy.
She's afraid of the *nighttime* noises outside.
The park is closed at *nighttime*.

gloss: The day or evening before an important day or event.
examples: They arrived on the *eve* of the wedding.
The team practiced hard on the *eve* of the big game.
Talks broke down on the *eve* of the deadline.

gloss: This present day.
examples: *Today* is my last day of work.
*Today* has been a long one.
The paper never came *today*.

gloss: The day after today.
examples: *Tomorrow* is supposed to be sunny.
Let's finish this *tomorrow*.
*Tomorrow* never seems to come.

gloss: The day before today.
examples: *Yesterday* was busier than usual.
I mailed the check *yesterday*.
It seems like *yesterday* that they were kids.

gloss: The night of the present day.
examples: *Tonight* is the season finale.
We're eating out *tonight*.
*Tonight* should be clear and cold.

gloss: Saturday and Sunday, when most people don't work.
examples: We're driving up for the *weekend*.
He works most *weekends*.
Have a good *weekend*.

gloss: Any day from Monday through Friday.
examples: The clinic is open on *weekdays* only.
Traffic is worse on a *weekday*.
She swims every *weekday* morning.

gloss: A day people go to work, or the hours worked in one day.
examples: My *workday* starts at seven.
It was a long *workday*.
Most *workdays* end around five.
contrast: Americans write *workday*; the British usually say *working day*.

gloss: The days and hours a person works in a week.
examples: They moved to a four-day *workweek*.
A standard *workweek* is forty hours.
Long *workweeks* wore him out.
contrast: American; the British say *working week*.

gloss: A day when most people don't work, usually to mark something.
examples: The bank is closed for the *holiday*.
Thanksgiving is my favorite *holiday*.
We get ten paid *holidays* a year.
contrast: In American English a *holiday* is a праздник; in British English it also means отпуск, which Americans call a *vacation*.

gloss: The yearly return of the date on which someone was born.
examples: Her *birthday* is in April.
We threw him a surprise *birthday* party.
The twins share the same *birthday*.

gloss: The yearly return of the date of a past event.
examples: They celebrated their tenth wedding *anniversary*.
The town marked the *anniversary* of the fire.
We never forget those two *anniversaries*.

gloss: A time of public celebration with music, food, or performances.
examples: The town holds a strawberry *festival* every June.
We saw three bands at the *festival*.
Summer *festivals* draw big crowds.

gloss: A large special meal, or a religious day of celebration.
examples: Grandma put together a real *feast*.
The village holds a *feast* after the harvest.
Their calendar is full of *feasts* and fasts.

gloss: A special anniversary, usually of twenty-five or fifty years.
examples: The college is planning its *jubilee*.
A parade marked the queen's *jubilee*.
Both *jubilees* drew thousands of visitors.
contrast: Stress the first syllable — JOO-buh-lee, unlike Russian «юбилЕй».

gloss: An important point or achievement along a longer path.
examples: Her first solo flight was a real *milestone*.
The baby has hit all the usual *milestones*.
Turning fifty felt like a *milestone*.

gloss: A plan or diagram showing when things happen, in order.
examples: Here's the *timeline* for the renovation.
The *timeline* lists every event of that year.
Both *timelines* end with the same deadline.

gloss: The order in which events happened, or a record of that order.
examples: The report includes a *chronology* of the accident.
Nobody could agree on the *chronology* of that night.
The book ends with a detailed *chronology*.
contrast: The ch is said like k, and the stress falls on the second syllable — kruh-NAH-luh-jee.

gloss: A book in which someone writes down what happens each day.
examples: She kept a *diary* all through high school.
His war *diary* was published years later.
Old *diaries* fill the bottom drawer.
contrast: For Americans a *diary* is a дневник; the British also use the word for ежедневник, which Americans call a *planner*.

gloss: A book or app for writing down appointments and tasks by date.
examples: She writes every assignment in her *planner*.
I bought a new *planner* for the school year.
Paper *planners* are popular again.

gloss: A list showing when things are supposed to happen.
examples: The train *timetable* changed in the spring.
We're behind on our *timetable*.
Both *timetables* were posted online.

gloss: Something that makes you remember to do something.
examples: Set a *reminder* on your phone.
The dentist sent a *reminder* about my appointment.
Sticky notes work better for me than digital *reminders*.

gloss: A count backward to the moment something starts.
examples: The *countdown* to launch began at noon.
Everyone joined the *countdown* to midnight.
The app runs *countdowns* for each exam.

gloss: The point at which something stops being valid.
examples: Check the *expiration* date on the milk.
The card is close to *expiration*.
*Expiration* of the lease is in June.
contrast: Americans say *expiration date*; the British say *expiry date*.

gloss: A year with an extra day in February, coming once every four years.
examples: This is a *leap year*, so February has twenty-nine days.
She was born on the last day of a *leap year*.
*Leap years* keep the calendar in step with the seasons.

gloss: A region in which all the clocks are set to the same time.
examples: The country spans four *time zones*.
I keep forgetting the *time zone* difference.
Set your phone to the local *time zone*.

gloss: The day of the week after Sunday, when the workweek usually starts.
examples: The report is due *Monday* morning.
Nobody around here likes *Mondays*.
We start the new schedule on *Monday*.

gloss: The day of the week between Tuesday and Thursday.
examples: Trash pickup is on *Wednesday*.
She has piano lessons every *Wednesday*.
Two *Wednesdays* a month the office closes early.
contrast: Spelled Wed-nes-day but said WENZ-day; the first d and the middle e are silent.

gloss: The day of the week between Wednesday and Friday.
examples: The show airs on *Thursday* nights.
We meet the first *Thursday* of every month.
*Thursdays* are always busy at the shop.

gloss: The day of the week between Thursday and Saturday.
examples: The office closes early on *Friday*.
Payday is every other *Friday*.
*Fridays* in summer are casual around here.

gloss: The day of the week between Friday and Sunday.
examples: We do laundry on *Saturday*.
The farmers market runs every *Saturday*.
He works most *Saturdays*.

gloss: The day of the week between Saturday and Monday.
examples: Dinner at my parents' is a *Sunday* tradition.
The paper is thickest on *Sunday*.
*Sundays* always feel too short.

gloss: The second month of the year, with twenty-eight or twenty-nine days.
examples: *February* is the coldest month here.
Her birthday falls in early *February*.
The last two *Februaries* were unusually mild.
contrast: Most Americans drop the first r — FEB-yoo-air-ee, not FEB-roo-air-ee.

gloss: The third month of the year.
examples: The snow usually melts by *March*.
We're moving at the end of *March*.
Spring break falls in *March* this year.

gloss: The fourth month of the year.
examples: Taxes are due in *April*.
*April* here means rain and mud.
The wedding is set for late *April*.

gloss: The fifth month of the year.
examples: Graduation is the third week of *May*.
The garden looks best in *May*.
We planted the tomatoes in early *May*.

gloss: The sixth month of the year.
examples: School lets out in *June*.
Most weddings around here are in *June*.
*June* was hotter than usual this year.

gloss: The seventh month of the year.
examples: We go to the lake every *July*.
*July* is the busiest month for the shop.
The fireworks are on the fourth of *July*.
contrast: The stress falls on the second syllable — juu-LY, unlike Russian «Июль».

gloss: The eighth month of the year.
examples: *August* is unbearably humid here.
The store has a big sale every *August*.
School starts in late *August*.
contrast: The month is AW-guhst; the rare adjective *august* (величественный) is aw-GUST.

gloss: The ninth month of the year.
examples: Classes start the first week of *September*.
*September* is my favorite month.
The leaves begin to turn in late *September*.

gloss: The tenth month of the year.
examples: The apples are ripe in *October*.
We turn the heat on in *October*.
Two *Octobers* ago we had snow before Halloween.

gloss: The eleventh month of the year.
examples: Elections are held in *November*.
*November* is gray and rainy here.
The lodge opens for the season in *November*.

gloss: The twelfth and last month of the year.
examples: *December* is our busiest month.
The days are shortest in late *December*.
We fly home every *December*.

gloss: A device or sound that wakes you up or warns you.
examples: My *alarm* goes off at six.
The fire *alarm* went off during class.
He sets three *alarms* every night.

gloss: A watch used to measure exactly how long something takes.
examples: The coach timed each lap with a *stopwatch*.
My phone has a *stopwatch* built in.
The two *stopwatches* showed different times.

gloss: A glass timer in which sand runs from the top half into the bottom.
examples: The board game came with a small *hourglass*.
The sand ran out of the *hourglass* in three minutes.
The shop sells antique *hourglasses*.
contrast: The h is silent, as in *hour* — OW-ur-glas.

gloss: A device that shows the time by the shadow the sun casts.
examples: There's a stone *sundial* in the garden.
A *sundial* is useless on a cloudy day.
Old gardens often have *sundials*.

gloss: A hanging weight that swings back and forth, often to keep a clock running.
examples: The *pendulum* in the hall clock stopped.
He watched the *pendulum* swing for a while.
Grandfather clocks use heavy *pendulums*.

gloss: The marked face of a clock or a round control you turn.
examples: The watch has a plain black *dial*.
Turn the *dial* to set the oven.
The old radio had two *dials* on the front.

gloss: A ringing sound made by a clock or a set of bells.
examples: The clock struck the hour with a soft *chime*.
We could hear the *chimes* of the church bells.
Their doorbell has an old-fashioned *chime*.

gloss: A short light sleep, or the alarm button that delays waking up.
examples: He took a quick *snooze* after lunch.
I hit *snooze* three times this morning.
Short *snoozes* just leave me groggy.

gloss: A short period of rest from work or activity.
examples: Let's take a ten-minute *break*.
She reads during her lunch *break*.
The teachers get two *breaks* a day.
contrast: *Break* and *brake* (тормоз) are perfect homophones in American English.

gloss: A break during a school day or a formal meeting.
examples: The kids play kickball at *recess*.
The judge called a short *recess*.
Congress is on summer *recess*.
contrast: Americans stress the first syllable — REE-ses; the British say ri-SESS.

gloss: A short break in the middle of a play, concert, or movie.
examples: We got drinks at *intermission*.
The play has one twenty-minute *intermission*.
Both *intermissions* were short.
contrast: The American word; the British call the same break an *interval*.

gloss: A short stop in speaking or in doing something.
examples: There was a long *pause* before she answered.
He spoke with awkward *pauses*.
After a brief *pause*, the music started again.
contrast: *Pause* and *paws* (лапы) sound exactly alike.

gloss: A period of waiting caused by something running late.
examples: Snow caused a two-hour *delay*.
There were long *delays* at the airport.
The work is going ahead without further *delay*.

gloss: An empty stretch of time between two things.
examples: There's a three-year *gap* between the sisters.
He took a *gap* year before college.
Fill the *gaps* in your schedule with study time.

gloss: A quiet period between busier ones.
examples: We fixed the roof during a *lull* in the storm.
There was a *lull* in the conversation.
Business has *lulls* every January.

gloss: A short break from something difficult or unpleasant.
examples: The rain gave us a brief *respite* from the heat.
Caregivers need a *respite* now and then.
There was no *respite* from the noise all week.
contrast: Americans say RES-pit, with the stress up front; the British often say ri-SPYT.

gloss: A pause during which something stops for a while.
examples: The band is on *hiatus* until next spring.
She came back to work after a two-year *hiatus*.
The show returned from its *hiatus* in June.

gloss: A wait between two flights or legs of a trip.
examples: We have a four-hour *layover* in Atlanta.
Short *layovers* are risky in winter.
I slept through the whole *layover*.
contrast: American; the British say *stopover*.

gloss: Time when work stops, or free time for resting.
examples: The outage caused hours of *downtime*.
I need some *downtime* this weekend.
There's very little *downtime* on this job.

gloss: A short break called during a game or activity.
examples: The coach called a *timeout*.
Each team gets three *timeouts* per half.
She put her son in *timeout* for hitting.

gloss: The break in the middle of a sports game.
examples: The band plays at *halftime*.
We were down by ten at *halftime*.
*Halftime* lasts fifteen minutes.
contrast: The l is silent — HAF-tym, just as in *half*.

gloss: The stretch of time between two events.
examples: In the *interim*, keep working on the draft.
Nothing much changed in the *interim*.
She ran the department in the *interim*.

ru: промежуток времени (in the meantime — тем временем)
gloss: The time between now and some later event.
examples: The doctor is running late; in the *meantime*, fill out this form.
Dinner is at eight; in the *meantime*, help yourself to bread.
We move in Friday, and in the *meantime* we're staying with friends.

gloss: The period and conditions that follow a bad event.
examples: The town rebuilt in the *aftermath* of the flood.
In the *aftermath*, everyone looked for someone to blame.
The *aftermath* of the storm dragged on for months.

gloss: The time when someone usually goes to sleep.
examples: It's past your *bedtime*.
We read a story every night at *bedtime*.
The two kids have different *bedtimes*.

gloss: The time in the middle of the day when people eat lunch.
examples: Call me at *lunchtime*.
The line gets long right around *lunchtime*.
He skipped *lunchtime* to finish the report.

gloss: The time in the evening when people eat dinner.
examples: Be home by *dinnertime*.
The phone always rings at *dinnertime*.
We talk about our day at *dinnertime*.

gloss: A rule requiring people to be home or off the streets by a set time.
examples: My *curfew* was eleven o'clock in high school.
The city set a *curfew* after the flooding.
Both towns lifted their *curfews* last week.

gloss: The season of spring.
examples: The orchard is beautiful in *springtime*.
*Springtime* here means mud and rain.
They always visit in the *springtime*.

gloss: The season of summer.
examples: In the *summertime* we swim every day.
*Summertime* traffic near the beach is terrible.
The shop stays open later in *summertime*.

gloss: The season of winter.
examples: The mountain road is closed in *wintertime*.
*Wintertime* means shoveling every week.
Heating bills double in the *wintertime*.

gloss: A period during which a country is at war.
examples: Her grandmother grew up in *wartime*.
*Wartime* rationing limited sugar and gas.
These photographs date from *wartime*.

gloss: A period during which a country is not at war.
examples: The base was quiet in *peacetime*.
*Peacetime* budgets are much smaller.
He served in both war and *peacetime*.

gloss: The time of a person's life when they are a child.
examples: She had a happy *childhood* on a farm.
*Childhood* friends still write to him.
Their *childhoods* could not have been more different.

gloss: The earliest period of a baby's life.
examples: He was adopted in *infancy*.
The condition is usually caught in *infancy*.
The technology is still in its *infancy*.

gloss: The years between childhood and adulthood.
examples: *Adolescence* was rough for both of them.
The book is about a boy in early *adolescence*.
Sleep patterns change during *adolescence*.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: The time when someone is young, or, as a countable noun, a young person.
examples: He played guitar in his *youth*.
Three *youths* were seen leaving the store.
The program keeps *youth* out of trouble after school.

gloss: The part of life after a person has grown up.
examples: She reached *adulthood* before her parents divorced.
Many friendships fade in *adulthood*.
The illness usually appears in early *adulthood*.

gloss: The best and strongest years of someone's life or career.
examples: He was a great runner in his *prime*.
The company is past its *prime*.
She's in the *prime* of her career.

gloss: The period when someone or something was most successful.
examples: In its *heyday*, the mill employed two thousand people.
The theater's *heyday* was in the 1930s.
Radio drama had its *heyday* long before television.

gloss: Ancient times, especially the age of Greece and Rome.
examples: The custom dates back to *antiquity*.
Scholars of *antiquity* still argue about the text.
Olive oil has been traded since *antiquity*.

gloss: A line of rulers or leaders from the same family.
examples: The *dynasty* ruled for three hundred years.
That team built a *dynasty* in the 1990s.
Several *dynasties* rose and fell in the valley.
contrast: Americans say DY-nuh-stee; the British say DIN-uh-stee.

gloss: The period during which a king or queen rules.
examples: The cathedral was built during her *reign*.
His *reign* lasted only two years.
Both *reigns* ended in war.
contrast: *Reign*, *rain* and *rein* (повод) all sound exactly alike.

gloss: The time before now.
examples: You can't change the *past*.
In the *past*, letters took weeks to arrive.
She rarely talks about her *past*.

gloss: The time that is happening now.
examples: Try to live in the *present*.
Up to the *present*, nobody has complained.
The *present* is all we really have.
contrast: The noun is PREZ-uhnt; the verb *present* (представлять) is pri-ZENT.

gloss: The time that is still to come.
examples: Nobody knows what the *future* holds.
In the near *future* we'll need a bigger office.
She's saving for the *future*.

gloss: Time without end, or a period that feels endless.
examples: The wait felt like an *eternity*.
They promised to love each other for *eternity*.
Those ten minutes seemed like an *eternity*.

gloss: How often something happens.
examples: The storms are increasing in *frequency*.
He calls home with surprising *frequency*.
The *frequency* of the meetings dropped to once a month.

gloss: A regular way of doing things in the same order.
examples: My morning *routine* takes about an hour.
The kids do better with a *routine*.
New *routines* take a few weeks to stick.
contrast: The stress falls on the second syllable — roo-TEEN, unlike Russian «рутИна», and the English word is neutral, not negative.

gloss: The habit of arriving or doing things exactly on time.
examples: *Punctuality* matters a lot in this office.
He's known for his *punctuality*.
Her *punctuality* has slipped since the baby came.

gloss: The habit of being late.
examples: The school sent a letter about her *tardiness*.
Repeated *tardiness* can cost you the job.
*Tardiness* counts against his grade.

gloss: The quality of needing to be dealt with right away.
examples: There's a real *urgency* to fixing the roof.
He spoke with growing *urgency*.
The letter had a note of *urgency* to it.

gloss: The state of needing to move or act fast.
examples: What's the *hurry*?
We left the house in a *hurry*.
There's no *hurry* — take your time.

gloss: A period of hurrying, or a sudden busy stretch of time.
examples: Avoid the morning *rush* if you can.
There's no *rush* on the paperwork.
The store hires extra help for the holiday *rush*.

gloss: A period spent waiting for something.
examples: It was a two-hour *wait* at the clinic.
The *wait* for a table was worth it.
Long *waits* frustrate customers.
contrast: *Wait* and *weight* (вес) are perfect homophones in American English.

gloss: A particular time when something happens, often a special one.
examples: We save this wine for special *occasions*.
I've met him on several *occasions*.
Her graduation was quite an *occasion*.

gloss: Something that happens, especially something planned or important.
examples: The fundraiser is our biggest *event* of the year.
*Events* moved faster than anyone expected.
In the *event* of rain, we'll move indoors.

gloss: The beginning of something, usually something unpleasant.
examples: The *onset* of winter came early this year.
Symptoms appear within days of *onset*.
The *onset* of the illness was sudden.

gloss: The very beginning of something.
examples: From the *outset*, the plan was too expensive.
She warned us at the *outset*.
At the *outset* nobody knew what to expect.

gloss: The first part or point of something.
examples: Start at the *beginning* of the chapter.
The *beginning* of the movie is slow.
Great companies often have humble *beginnings*.

gloss: The point at which something begins.
examples: We got off to a bad *start*.
The race has a staggered *start*.
After two false *starts*, the engine caught.

gloss: The final part or point of something.
examples: Stay until the *end* of the meeting.
Rent is due at the *end* of the month.
Both *ends* of the trip went smoothly.

gloss: The period during which someone holds a job or an office.
examples: Crime fell during her *tenure* as mayor.
He earned *tenure* after six years of teaching.
His *tenure* at the company was short.

gloss: A long break from work, usually for study or travel.
examples: She's on *sabbatical* in Italy this year.
The professor took a *sabbatical* to finish his book.
Few companies offer *sabbaticals*.

gloss: A period when workers are sent home without pay, or leave granted to a soldier.
examples: Thousands of staff were put on *furlough*.
He came home on a two-week *furlough*.
The *furloughs* ended when the funding came through.
contrast: The ough is said like oh — FUR-loh, not FUR-luff.

gloss: A trial period at a new job, or supervision ordered instead of prison.
examples: New hires are on *probation* for ninety days.
He got two years of *probation* instead of jail.
She finished her *probation* without a single complaint.
